section1.heading: To you... who wants everything to be perfect
section1.content: FOUR PERFECTIONISTS is a book I chose because I felt I was a perfectionist, but didn't know if it was a good or bad thing. It raised many questions: How many types of perfectionists are there? Which one am I? And how can I use my perfectionist traits to my advantage?

section2.heading: Getting to know yourself
section2.content: In this article, we will get to know ourselves and our own perfectionism to transform into 'Excellent Perfectionists.' I have summarized this into 4 main topics: Addressing the exhaustion of perfectionism, how perfectionists are born, the 4 types of perfectionists, and how to change into an excellent perfectionist.

section3.heading: Chapter 1
section3.content: In Chapter 1, we explore the pursuit of perfection among perfectionists.

section4.heading: The Desire for Perfection
section4.content01: The mindset of: Must do better than others, must never make a mistake, must be the most perfect.
section4.content02: Perfectionists often fail because they set goals too high. When they don't succeed, they blame themselves, which can lead to depression.
section4.content03: A survey shows 7 out of 10 employees are perfectionists and believe it has a positive effect on work efficiency.
section4.content05: ...when asked: 'Does being a perfectionist make you happy?'

section5.heading: The Unhappy Perfectionist
section5.content: An unhappy perfectionist might say, 'If I had taken the subway instead of a taxi, I wouldn't have faced this problem.' Even when the cause is an external factor, they still blame themselves.

section6.heading: The Happy Perfectionist
list: Uses perfectionism to achieve goals | Does not dwell on mistakes
Flexible in the process of reaching goals | Controls their own inner drive
Views failure positively | May not get a perfect score, but solved the problem

section7.heading: Chapter 2
section7.content: In Chapter 2, we look at the 5 factors that turn you into a perfectionist.

section8.heading: Identifying Our Perfectionism
list: Excessive worry about mistakes
Organizing habits
High parental expectations
High standards for success
Self-doubt in actions

section9.heading: Factor 1: Excessive worry about mistakes
section9.content01: A. Spending too much time fixing a small typo while forgetting the more important task: submitting the work on time.
section9.content02: B. Planning a holiday so perfectly out of fear that it won't be perfect.

section10.heading: The Fear of Making Mistakes
section10.description: The fear of mistakes is divided into 2 types:
list: Trying your best not to repeat a mistake.
Being obsessed and overly worried about repeating a mistake.

section11.heading: Factor 2: Organizing habits
list: Making a cross sign before entering an interview room.
Swinging the club several times before a game.
Needing to spin a pen before being able to do an exam.
Organizing the desk before starting a report.
Checking glasses when stuck on a thought.
Being rushed and having no time to organize | Feeling a loss of control.
Organizing until the goal is forgotten and energy is depleted.

section12.heading: Factor 3: High parental expectations
list: 30 out of 37 people say their perfectionism came from their parents.
The feeling of: 'Is this all you can do?' (Anxiety from not meeting parents' standards).
Getting 80 on a test and seeing the subtle disappointment on a parent's face.
Getting 100 on a test and seeing the mood change completely.

section13.heading: Factor 4: High standards for success
list: My own standards vs. the standards I think others expect.
If friends once teased you about your clothes, you might still worry about dressing up.
Chasing a goal without knowing if it's truly your own.
For perfectionists following their own high standards, others' opinions are just 'suggestions.'

section14.heading: Factor 5: Self-doubt in actions
list: Thinking 'Can I really do this?' or 'Is this truly the best?'
Hearing 'Ready, set, go' and wondering 'Did I hear the signal correctly?'
Choosing between: A 100% chance to get 40,000 Baht.
Or an 80% chance to get 50,000 Baht.

section15.heading: From these choices
section15.content: There are those who doubt themselves to avoid losing out, and those who are daring because they believe in their own ability and flexibility.

section16.heading: Chapter 3
section16.content: In Chapter 3, we learn the starting point for understanding your own and others' perfectionism.

section17.heading: Locus of Evaluation and Self-Control Focus
section17.content: We categorize perfectionists using two axes: Locus of Evaluation and Self-Control Focus.

section18.heading: Locus of Evaluation
list: Internal => Focus on personal values / self-evaluation based on own methods.
External => Focus on others' reactions and judgments / evaluating self based on others.

section19.heading: Self-Control Focus
list: Promotion => Enthusiastic, likes challenges / 'It's hard work, but I'll rest soon.'
Prevention => Avoids predictable risks / doesn't want to start new projects for fear of being disliked.

section20.heading: The 4 Types of Perfectionists
section20.content: By combining Locus of Evaluation and Self-Control Focus, we can identify 4 types of perfectionists:

section25.heading: Type 1: Approval-seeker
section25.description: Skilled at reading situations and relationships:
list: Maintains relationships and checks in on others to avoid being distant.
Happiest when hearing: 'Only you could do this' or 'We couldn't do this without you.'
Small problems cause immediate disappointment and sadness.
Advice: Dare to say 'no'; think carefully about what others ask of you.
Advice: Show your true self; you will earn even more trust.

section26.heading: Type 2: Thrill-seeker
section26.description: Likes the rush, often works at the last minute:
list: Waiting for 100% inspiration before starting—but that time never really comes.
If given 6 months, starts in the last 2 months; if it's too late, they might quit.
Comfortable with short sprints but struggles with marathons.
Advice: Develop a 'Time Perspective' and better time estimation.
Advice: Have a clear picture of what to do and when to reduce uncertainty.

section27.heading: Type 3: Safety-first
list: Travels abroad with an absolutely perfect itinerary.
When sending emails, focuses so much on content they forget the recipient's feelings.
Never fails because of constant caution, but feels sad because they never feel excitement.
Advice: Reduce caution appropriately to feel more excited about work.
Advice: Express yourself more; that is part of being human.

section28.heading: Type 4: Growth-oriented
list: Very excited when starting new work; does not hesitate to face challenges.
Chases uncertain goals, challenges self regularly, and doesn't get discouraged.
Self-esteem prevents others' attitudes from destroying them.
Advice: Learn to accept 'conflict' at an appropriate level.
Advice: Don't show boredom; show empathy toward others.

section29.heading: Chapter 4
section29.content: Chapter 4 discusses practical guidelines for change and growth.

section30.heading: Transformation
list: Record events that trigger your pursuit of perfection.
Express both positive and negative emotions.
Ask yourself: 'If I could go back, what words of encouragement would I give myself?'

section31.heading: For Approval-seekers
section31.description: Should focus more on their own heart than others':
list: Explain in detail what you 'like.' Write it down and categorize it.
Write down what you are good at and what you want to improve in the future.

section32.heading: For Thrill-seekers
section32.description: Should develop a realistic perception of time:
list: Record estimated time vs. actual time spent on tasks.
Analyze the causes of discrepancies carefully.
Learn to reduce errors and try not to repeat them.
Prepare detailed plans for tasks no longer than 15 minutes.

section33.heading: For Safety-first types
list: Look back to find the reasons why you missed an opportunity.
Practice growth-oriented speech.

section34.heading: For Growth-oriented types
section34.description: Should focus on building relationships with others:
list: Listen to others' experiences and opinions.
Maintain a friendly and positive attitude toward others.
Respond to others honestly.

section35.heading: Summary
section35.content: A final look at the 4 types of perfectionists:

section36.heading: Approval-seeker (Summary)
list: External Locus x Promotion Focus.
Easily liked by others.
But has an extreme level of perfectionism.
Often neglects themselves because they are too busy caring for others.

section37.heading: Thrill-seeker (Summary)
list: External Locus x Prevention Focus.
Good at solving immediate problems.
Tends to procrastinate on important tasks.
Fears failure and negative evaluation.

section38.heading: Safety-first (Summary)
list: Internal Locus x Prevention Focus.
Works meticulously and with dedication.
Often avoids change or challenges.
Prefers to maintain the status quo.

section39.heading: Growth-oriented (Summary)
list: Internal Locus x Promotion Focus.
Confident and has proactive leadership.
Often considered the happiest type of perfectionist.

section40.heading: Pursuing Perfection
section40.content: Perfection is not a small thing, but perfection is made of small things.

section41.heading: To you... who wants everything to be perfect
section41.content: I hope this summary is useful. Don't forget to grab a copy of 'Four Perfectionists' to read in full. This article is for you... who wants everything to be perfect. *-*
